newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Brazilian soil holds untapped wealth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brazilian soil holds untapped wealth.

text.p: Yet another report of a potentially major gold and copper discovery hit Brazil's press this week but to one man, the possibility of huge deposits of gold and other minerals beneath Brazilian soil is old news.

"Brazil is the country which, together with China, holds the greatest potential for mineral discoveries in the coming years," said Carlos Oiti Berbert, director-president of geological survey company, Mineral Resources Exploration Company (CPRM).
"Around 80 percent of current Brazilian mines are open-pit so we haven't even reached the subsoil yet," he added.
The CPRM, founded by the government in August 1969, has an important goal - the knowledge of Brazil's soil and subsoil, its geology and mineral potential.
In the last 27 years, it has developed more than 300 exploration projects, resulting in opportunities for investors in minerals such as tin, coal, limestone and gold.

According to a 1996 report by the Mines and Energy Ministry, Brazil in 1995 was estimated to possess 88.3 percent of the world's niobium reserves, 14.1 percent of all kaolin, 13.6 percent of bauxite and 7.2 percent of tin reserves.

In recent years, gold has been the headline grabber, the most notable being an announcement last February by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso of the Serra Leste gold mine in northern Para state, which could have reserves of 150 tonnes.
Earlier this week, a local newspaper ran a page one story on an "historic" discovery of gold and copper deposits by state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce which also owns the Serra Leste mine.

CVRD maintained the report was confusing information passed to the market in October last year when it reported "promising" results from a small number of drill holes but stressed it was too early to talk of discoveries, small or otherwise.
Brazil has already hosted the largest gold rush in history when up to one million garimpeiros or wild-cat miners invaded a site in the 1980s very near Serra Leste.

But since Brazil changed its constitution in the second half of 1995 ending limits on foreign participation in Brazilian companies, the country is seeing another flood of interest - this time from international mining companies, Berbert said.

"Since March 1995, we started to see an increase in interest because people had already started to expect the change in the constitution. From then on, I have received two or three inquiries a week from international firms and especially in the last 12 months," Berbert said.
In coming years, the main mineral discoveries in Brazil are likely to be of diamonds, gold, lead, nickel and tin, he added.
At present, about 70 percent of interest is from Canadian companies, 20 to 25 percent from U.S. firms and the remaining five percent from companies from Australia, the U.K and South Africa, he added.
"I think things will change in the coming years and that the number of Australian and South African companies will increase as well as Japanese and Korean firms," Berbert said.

While now concentrating on environmental issues and geological surveys, particularly in the Amazon area, the CPRM will this year also be involved in auctioning rights to several areas for which it assumed responsibility in the 1970s.
The first area is a possible gold reserve in Rondonia state and initial surveys show the area could contain between 15 and 30 tonnes of gold.

Companies which have already expressed interest in the site include Canada's Barrick Gold ABX.TOu, Anglo-Australian RTZ-CRA RTZ.L and South Africa's Gencor. Firms interested in winning the exploration rights have until February 3 to submit a proposal to the CPRM.
Other possible gold sites to be auctioned are the Eldorado and Vale do Ribeira projects both in Sao Paulo state and also the Natividade project in the northern state of Tocantins.
"We want to do everything possible to complete these four and others by July this year," Herbert said.
One of the largest projects is a 494 million tonne kaolin deposit in Para state which is the "purest known kaolin discovered to this day," Berbert said.
CPRM owns around 50 percent of the rights to this deposit but "it will require large investments so international participation will be needed", he added.
